insider_note: The sum x + y appears both as the argument of the exponential AND is exactly what dy/dx + 1 becomes once t = x + y is introduced — that double appearance is the signal to substitute t = x + y rather than trying to separate x and y directly.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Substitute t = x + y
steps.margin_note: One mark. Put t = x + y, so dt/dx = 1 + dy/dx — exactly the left side of the given equation.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever dy/dx + 1 sits next to e^(x+y), recognise dt/dx = 1 + dy/dx for t = x + y and the equation collapses to a single variable.
lines: Put x + y = t. Then 1 + dy/dx = dt/dx
steps.why: Setting t = x + y makes dt/dx equal to 1 + dy/dx by the chain rule, which is exactly the left-hand side of the given equation, so the whole equation collapses to a single separable equation in t and x alone.
common_mistakes: Writing dt/dx = dy/dx instead of dt/dx = 1 + dy/dx, forgetting the derivative of x itself contributes 1.
Trying to separate x and y directly without first spotting the t = x + y substitution.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Separate as e^(−t)dt = dx, integrate to −e^(−t) = x + c, then put t = x + y back in.
steps.memory_tip: ∫e^(−t)dt = −e^(−t) — the same negative-exponential integral that appears whenever the equation separates into e^(−t)dt = dx.
steps.why: Separating the variables in t and x and integrating gives −e^(−t) = x + c; moving every term to one side and substituting t = x + y back in gives the final relation entirely in the original variables.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to substitute t = x + y back into the final answer and leaving it in terms of t.
Dropping the minus sign on e^(−t) when moving it across, writing e^(−(x+y)) = x + c instead of e^(−(x+y)) + x + c = 0.
